title: The source tree has six directories, one purpose each: abi, kernel, hal and the leaf crates (lib) are the new kernel, boot holds the boot loaders, and bsd holds the whole LandingZone tree still being replaced, so deleting it at N9 is one directory; every count, test and smoke equal before and after the move

The device tree reader is the kernel's (N7.2b0): every read of the boot loader's tree is bounds-checked, the boot refuses a tree placed in usable memory, and boot(8)'s softraid key is copied and wiped before the tree is shared, where a review found the old order wrote behind a read-only view

The leaf crates are grouped by purpose like the rest of the kernel: sysdefs, the kernel's domain model of OpenBSD's types and structures, by the kernel's own groups (proc, file, net, netinet, ...), libkern in strings, memory, hashes and random, libz in deflate, inflate and checksums; a check keeps their roots to groups only

OpenBSD's basic types, constants and the structures userland shares now live in one leaf crate, sysdefs, that every layer uses instead of each inventing its own; the kernel's library crates (libkern, libz, sysdefs) hold no unsafe, and measurements since N6 show no slowdown: reading files, pipes, boot and page faults equal, fork and exec faster

The disk layer is the kernel's (labels, disk statistics, diskmap and the choice of the root device), with each I/O finding its disk without a lock as in OpenBSD; and the hardware layer no longer interprets a system call: it hands the system-call layer a safe view of the trap's registers, and abi owns OpenBSD's arm64 convention with named registers; the LandingZone tree falls to 6,907 unsafe

The system-call layer calls the kernel directly: the table of function pointers that sat in the hardware layer is gone, abi is split by the kernel's groups and checked to call nothing but the kernel's one door; and boot -c's device editor (userconf) is the kernel's, its dialogue unchanged

The kernel's code is now ordered by purpose: the hardware layer's modules in six groups (locks, memory, data structures, the processor, virtual memory and devices, the only group drivers use), the safe kernel crate's in eight (processes, scheduler, signals, time, files, terminals, base services, devices), and a check that keeps drivers out of the hardware layer; a pure move, with the same unsafe count before and after; next, the system-call layer calls the kernel directly instead of through a table in the hardware layer

N7, devices, starts: its first three slices are on main with every check green — typed device registers and DMA memory in the hardware layer, autoconfiguration in the safe kernel crate, and the small device services (event counters, sensors, the watchdog, the clock helpers); the LandingZone tree falls to 6,971 unsafe

N6's close checks are green and on main: just check (6153 host tests), just ci and just ci-full with the installers pass, and the comparison with a real OpenBSD gives 153 of 156 steps equal, 3 expected and 0 unexpected, with the nfs scenarios run for the first time; the runs found and fixed three real bugs (re(4) programming its multicast filter before its Ethernet attach, a smoke racing the virtio GPU's refresh, and a network probe with no loopback address) and two test bugs (a benchmark calling ARP without the net lock, a test releasing a buffer into another test's cache); netstat(1) now runs in the smokes and pf's tables are tested; the boot banner prints the code name "Arica"; N6 is declared met once the user rules on nine benchmarks that rose more than 10 % and on the exit criterion's wording; meanwhile N7, devices, is planned in 22 slices and its first three are written and reviewed

N6.7 done: the nfs server is the kernel's (N6.7b4): nfssvc is now a native system call (190 of 331) and the old server's 11 files are deleted (57 fewer unsafe); pf's tables and IPsec's policies run on the kernel's own radix tree (N6.7b1), whose old copy is deleted too (86 fewer unsafe), at 34.5 ns per table lookup against the old tree's 24.4 after two rounds of layout work the user chose; along the way the review found that OpenBSD's pf reads its tables while other CPUs change them, uses an entry after it may be freed, and counts with plain increments from every CPU: the kernel now guards each table with a read-write lock, keeps it held while an entry is used, and counts atomically, at +6 % per lookup; the LandingZone tree is down to 7017 unsafe; next is N6's close

N6.7b3 done: the nfs server's procedures are the kernel's (read, write, lookup, create, rename, readdir and the rest), built beside the old server and switched on at N6.7b4; every wire length is checked before use and every permission check of OpenBSD kept in its order; the review found no code defect, and the tests now cover NFSv2, reads and writes across many network buffers, and unmount after each test so a leaked file would show; two OpenBSD bugs on the list: an exclusive create that never stores its verifier on 64-bit machines, and a read reply leaked on an error path; 5896 host tests green

N6.7b2 done: the nfs server's core is the kernel's, built beside the old one (switched on at N6.7b4): request parsing with every wire length checked before use, the duplicate request cache, the socket receive path and the nfsd loop; the review found no blocker and four fixes, among them a window at server restart where OpenBSD's own code can use freed memory, closed here; 19 of 19 mutations caught; pf's and IPsec's radix tree got 59 % faster (80 -> 33 ns per table lookup) and is under review with the server's procedures (N6.7b1, b3)

N6.7a done: the nfs client is the kernel's and the one that runs (N6.7a5): mounting, unmounting, statfs and the diskless root now go through safe kernel code, and the old client's 11 files are deleted from the LandingZone tree (56 fewer unsafe, 7216 -> 7160); the nfs smoke now also checks a symlink, a 256 KiB write, a rename, removing an open file and an NFSv2 mount, and a new comparison set against real OpenBSD runs at N6's close; the review asked to keep OpenBSD's order of the memory pools (vmstat -m) and to test mount(2)'s argument checks, both done; the nfs server (N6.7b) stays paused for now

N6.7a3 done: the nfs client's file operations are the kernel's (open, read, write, lookup, create, rename, readdir and the rest of nfs_vnops, with the read and write paths through the buffer cache), built beside the old client and switched on next in N6.7a5; the review found two real bugs and both are fixed: an NFSv3 write no longer leaves the client's copy of the file's time stale (every reopen threw away the cache), and a server that answers a transfer size of 0 can no longer crash the kernel, where OpenBSD's own code traps or reads past its buffer; 36 new tests, 5883 host tests green; N6.7a is 5 of 6

N6.6b done: raw IP, raw IPv6 and divert(4) are now the kernel's (N6.6b1): the safe code is in OpenBSD's protocol tables and the old files are deleted, with ICMP's raw tail calling the kernel directly as OpenBSD does and kern.file locking each socket through the kernel's own pair; reviewed against OpenBSD's code, nothing blocking; 25 fewer unsafe in the LandingZone tree (7241 -> 7216, netinet6 down to 1); the boot, IPv6, ESP and divert smokes passed after the switch and 6150 host tests are green

Four more nfs parts and the radix tree are the kernel's: the nfs client's RPC engine (N6.7a1, tested against a real kernel socket on loopback), its node table, attribute cache and buffer queue (N6.7a2), the diskless boot (N6.7a4), and a radix tree that owns its nodes with the NFS export list (N6.7b0). The export check now copies the anonymous credential by value, closing a window where OpenBSD can read an export entry another thread frees; the radix tree repairs a state where OpenBSD's radix.c reads freed memory (no caller reaches it today). Every part reviewed against OpenBSD's code; 15 fewer unsafe in the LandingZone tree (7256 -> 7241); 6130 host tests green after a test-isolation fix; the client's file operations, pf and IPsec on the new tree and the nfs server are being written

N6.7a0 done: the nfs client's wire format, its XDR encoding and decoding, the RPC transaction ids and the nfs constants userland shares are the kernel's, as safe code, beside the old client until the switch; reviewed against OpenBSD's code, its fixes checked; 16 fewer unsafe in the LandingZone tree (7272 -> 7256) and 6017 host tests green; raw sockets and divert, the nfs RPC engine, the diskless boot and the typed radix tree for the nfs exports are being built in parallel

UDP is now the kernel's (N6.6b0): the safe UDP for IPv4 and IPv6 replaced the old one, with IPsec's UDP checks and wg(4)'s upcall as safe code (wg lost its unsafe there), 40 fewer unsafe in the LandingZone tree (7312 -> 7272); reviewed against OpenBSD's code, nothing blocking; the boot, nfs, wg and pfsync smokes passed after the switch and 5989 host tests are green; raw sockets and divert are switching next, and the nfs client and server are being built in parallel. Also: Kernel now pins LandingZone at e8249449, all 59 commits since the first pin triaged

sysarch(2) answers EINVAL as on OpenBSD instead of killing the caller: LandingZone ported it and the kernel took it by sync as safe code, its amd64 half kept for N10 (one inherited unsafe, counted); reviewed, nothing blocking; host tests green; every LandingZone commit after the pin is now triaged (59 of 59)

TCP is now the kernel's: the switch (N6.6a5) put the safe TCP in OpenBSD's protocol table and deleted the old one, 83 fewer unsafe in the LandingZone tree (7394 -> 7311); reviewed against OpenBSD's code path by path, nothing blocking; at the review a cost OpenBSD does not pay (a counter on every read and write of a TCP socket) was removed instead of postponed; the boot, TCP and multiprocessor network smokes passed after the switch, the host tests are green after the review's fixes, and every smoke runs again at the N6 close; next is N6.6b, UDP, raw sockets and divert

__thrsleep and __thrwakeup, the calls OpenBSD's threads sleep and wake on, are in: LandingZone ported them and the kernel took them by sync as safe code (LandingZone's port had 5 unsafe, this one has none); reviewed against OpenBSD's code path by path, nothing blocking; 5679 host tests green; the smoke that exercises them runs at the N6 close; next is 6a5, the switch to the kernel's TCP

N6.6a4 done: TCP's input path, its option parsing and the SYN cache's accept path are the kernel's, still beside the old TCP until the switch at 6a5; two reviews: the first caught a handshake answered with a reset where OpenBSD completes it (a second listener bound mid-handshake), now completed as OpenBSD does, with the SYN's timestamp kept so fast-path prediction and PAWS work; signature checks compared in constant time; no unsafe added, 5665 host tests green

First large sync with LandingZone's debt milestone TD0: 48 commits triaged, 43 recorded so far (the rest are __thrsleep and sysarch, next); its arm64 security fix taken as a boot-time check that no kernel mapping is executable from user mode; a boot fault on processors with SVE fixed (OpenBSD's own slip, handed to LandingZone, which adopted it); and the kernel now boots the real userland to a root shell under Apple's hypervisor in 7 seconds

N6.6a3 done: TCP's output path, its retransmit, persist, keep-alive and delayed-ACK timers, connection drop and ICMP handling (including path MTU discovery) are the kernel's, still beside the old TCP until the switch at 6a5; signed segments now tested byte for byte against an independent MD5, IPv6 segments too; a SACK-with-signature request answers EINVAL in every build, as OpenBSD's shipped kernel does; no unsafe added, 5623 host tests green; 6a4 under way

N6.6a2 done: TCP's control block, its timers' entry, reassembly, SACK and the first half of the SYN cache are the kernel's, built beside the old TCP until the switch at 6a5; TCP MD5 signatures checked against an independent MD5, and the per-connection pcb trimmed back to 568 bytes by sharing one cell for IPv4 and IPv6 multicast options, as OpenBSD's union does; no unsafe added, 5580 host tests green; 6a3 under way

N6.6a1 done: TCP's state machine, sequence arithmetic, per-CPU statistics, soft LRO, software TSO and the Toeplitz hash are the kernel's; the review caught a crafted short TCP header that would have panicked LRO once an LRO driver lands, fixed to read the header as OpenBSD does; bsd's unsafe 7419 -> 7394, 5552 host tests green; 6a2 under way

N6.6a0 done: TCP's groundwork is in: the socket lock every kernel TCP socket will take, two hal cells for mbuf chains (+2 unsafe, each with its proof), TCP's ABI structures checked byte for byte against the C headers, and the pf and IPsec entry points TCP needs; also: the kernel now builds with DevTools' new Rust, whose native tools were checked on a BTI processor; 5538 host tests green

N6.6a (TCP) planned: about 14,700 lines and 109 unsafe move in six serial parts, the kernel's TCP built beside the old one and switched on last, then checked once in QEMU and against real OpenBSD with a new TCP scenario; 6a0, the preconditions, under way

N6.5e done: multicast group records are counted too, so a group left for good is freed as in OpenBSD instead of kept linked for ever (records 112 -> 80 bytes); with 5e0 and 5e1, every interface and multicast address now lives exactly as long as its holders; no new unsafe, 5490 host tests green; N6.6a, TCP, starts with its survey
Code names: a new EmiBSD every six months, following OpenBSD, each named after a region of Chile from north to south; the first cycle, on OpenBSD 8.0, from 2026.11 to 2026.11.4 so far, is Arica

N6.5e1 done: IPv4 and IPv6 interface addresses are counted handles, freed when the last holder lets go as in OpenBSD; the review caught pf reading a netmask cut short where OpenBSD reads it whole, fixed with a test; bsd's unsafe 7433 -> 7420, 5484 host tests green; N6.5e2 (multicast) under way

N6.5e0 done: hal's net lock now guards cells a list can lend safely, through shared and exclusive witnesses; two reviews found and closed a hole where a proof of the lock could outlive another process's read hold, now every proof keeps its hold; no new unsafe (hal 225), 5475 host tests green

N6.5e planned and started: the interface-address and multicast records become counted handles, freed when the last holder lets go, in three parts (5e0 hal's net-lock cells, 5e1 addresses, 5e2 multicast); 5e0 written with no new unsafe and in review

After the N6.5 close: the last caller of bsd's if_output_mq moved, so it goes (bsd 7435 -> 7433 unsafe); clippy keeps the C's field names of seven structs; the IPv6 test fixtures reset their state; N6's record sizes listed for N12. Next: N6.5e, counted handles for the interface addresses

N6.5 closed: all of IPv6 is the kernel's, benchmarked against its start (packet delivery 51.8 -> 23.8 ns, reassembly 420.6 -> 221.1 ns, a neighbour miss 102.6 -> 53.9 ns; the rises named for N12) and linted; bsd 7713 -> 7435 unsafe over N6.5, 5427 host tests green

N6.5d done: IPv6 input, forwarding, fragment reassembly, ICMPv6 and the inet6 protocol table are the kernel's, so all of IPv6 is; every packet parser keeps OpenBSD's checks, each mutation-tested; bsd 7505 -> 7435 unsafe, 5426 host tests green

N6.5c done: the IPv6 output path, its 33 socket options and the control block's IPv6 half are the kernel's; every option check of OpenBSD's C kept and mutation-tested, fragments never copy a shared buffer; bsd 7592 -> 7505 unsafe, 5403 host tests green

N6.5b done: IPv6 neighbour discovery and duplicate address detection are the kernel's; ARP's and ND's records share one typed route slot without new unsafe, and every NS/NA rejection of OpenBSD's C is a tested table; bsd 7644 -> 7592 unsafe, 5384 host tests green

N6.5a done: IPv6 addresses, multicast records, MLD and source address selection are the kernel's; the address ioctls keep OpenBSD's checks and lock order, and MLD input is bounded by its own buffers; bsd 7713 -> 7644 unsafe, 5358 host tests green

N6.4 closed: IPv4 is the kernel's, benchmarked against its start (the loopback output path 55.5 -> 35.3 ns, packet delivery 37.4 -> 20.9 ns, an ARP miss 102.9 -> 49.0 ns; the rises named for N12) and linted; bsd 7928 -> 7713 unsafe over N6.4, 5325 host tests green

N6.4c2 done: IPv4 input, fragment reassembly, ICMP and the inet protocol table are the kernel's; every packet parser checks what OpenBSD's C checks, and the last legacy ICMP hand-off checks its own bounds; bsd 7770 -> 7713 unsafe, 5325 host tests green

N6.4c1 done: the protocol control block every IPv4 and IPv6 socket hangs on, and the IP socket options, are the kernel's; a lookup's reference is taken under the table's mutex as a type, and pf's word in a pcb is written only with pf's key; bsd 7821 -> 7770 unsafe, 5299 host tests green
N6.4b done: ARP is the kernel's, the route's link-level record a typed word, and the last bsd unsafe of the ARP path gone; bsd 7847 -> 7821 unsafe, 5281 host tests green
N6.4a done: the IPv4 addresses, multicast records, IGMP and the IPv4 output path are the kernel's, with the netinet headers and checksums; bsd 7928 -> 7847 unsafe
The kernel is synced with LandingZone up to 937d22ef: every commit after the pin triaged, none left open
N6.3c2 done: the Ethernet and loopback link layers are the kernel's, and the Link bridge to the LandingZone tree is gone; bsd 7967 -> 7928 unsafe
N6.3c1 done: bpf(4) and its filter machine are the kernel's, every per-packet row at or below LandingZone's; bsd 8013 -> 7967 unsafe
N6.3b2 done: the routing socket is the kernel's and the LandingZone tree routes through it; bsd 8416 -> 8013 unsafe
N6.3b1 done: the routing table (ART), its routes, multipath and route timers are the kernel's, ready to be wired

LLVM 23.1.4+emibsd.6 and Rust 1.99.1+emibsd.5, each as four artifacts: the toolchain that runs on the Mac and the native one that runs on EmiBSD, for arm64 and amd64. New: the profile and ubsan_minimal runtimes, the manual pages, rust-analyzer, the native cargo against the system's shared LibreSSL; on arm64 the native cc, c++, ar, rustc, cargo, clippy, rustfmt and rustdoc ran under the EmiBSD kernel in QEMU
The kernel is built with EmiBSD's own toolchain, DevTools' Rust and LLVM, run straight from their releases (decision 49)

The native toolchain: LLVM 23.1.4 and Rust 1.99.1 built to run on EmiBSD itself, one artifact per architecture, for the userland's comp set; on arm64, under the EmiBSD kernel in QEMU, the native cc, c++, ar and rustc built and ran their programs; amd64 is built and waits for the kernel's amd64 boot
N6.3a2 done: the interface ioctls and media are the kernel's
N6.3a1 done: the network interface core (ifnet, the interface queues, netisr) is the kernel's

The release 2026.11.4, a signed pre-release for arm64 that replaces 2026.11.3, whose ISO could not be rebuilt from its tag: the same Kernel 20261108-b99aedaf and Userland 2026.11.4, DevTools llvm-23.1.4+emibsd.4 and rust-1.99.1+emibsd.2; both media install in QEMU and boot to login:, and the tree is on cdn.emibsd.org

The release 2026.11.3, a signed pre-release for arm64: Kernel 20261108-b99aedaf, with the socket layer and the socket system calls in the new kernel, and Userland 2026.11.4, built against that kernel's ABI headers; both media install in QEMU and boot to login:, the tree is on cdn.emibsd.org, now browsable
N6.2b done: the socket system calls are handled natively by the kernel
N6.2a done: the socket layer and unix domain sockets, descriptor passing included, are the kernel's
N6.1 done: the mbuf, the packet buffer under the whole network stack, is the kernel's

The first signed release, 2026.11.2, a pre-release for arm64: the media are signed with EmiBSD's own signify key and the installer verifies the sets against it; Userland 2026.11.3, the base system renamed EmiBSD, on Kernel 20261107-b2a15ba6; the tree is also on the mirror, cdn.emibsd.org

The second release, 2026.11.1, a pre-release for arm64: Kernel 20261107-d2107de6, with the ABI linked into the kernel, and Userland 2026.11.2, whose base carries the same EFI loader the media boot from; both media install in QEMU and boot to login:

The ABI is linked into the kernel image (decision 47): the abi crate stays separate, forbid and without logic
N5.9 done: tmpfs and fuse are the kernel's; sys/tmpfs/ and sys/miscfs/ are deleted from the LandingZone tree

The first release, 2026.11, a pre-release for arm64: an install ISO and a USB stick image that install EmiBSD in QEMU with no network and boot it to login:; Kernel 20261106-ac41e133 and Userland 2026.11.1, not yet compared with a real OpenBSD

The install media: an ISO and a USB stick image for arm64, made in OS from Kernel's and Userland's releases; each installs EmiBSD in QEMU from its own sets with no network, the installed disk boots to login:, and two builds give the same sums
N5.8 done: cd9660 and udf are the kernel's, and sys/isofs/ is deleted from the LandingZone tree

The kernel's first release artifact for EmiBSD/OS (dist-arm64), the build OS's install media are made from

N5.6 done: ext2fs is the kernel's
The whole inherited base system builds for EmiBSD with its own make: 37 libraries and every program of bin, sbin, usr.bin, usr.sbin, libexec, share and games, and the base, comp, game and man sets
